claim: ACH did not improve human analysts' judgment accuracy or coherence in controlled tests.
note: Mandel 2018 (n=50), Dhami 2019 (n=50, probably same analyst pool, partly dependent), Karvetski and Mandel 2020 (n=227), Karvetski, Mandel, Irwin 2020. One author group throughout; no outside replication. Effects small and mostly p>.05, so 'no gain', not 'proven harm'.

claim: ACH may slightly reduce coherence or reliability (harm, not just no benefit).
note: p=.051, d=0.20 in one study; coherence loss in another; Mandel 2018 error gap p=.14. Direction consistent, significance weak.

claim: Forcing probabilities over exclusive hypotheses to sum to 1 cuts error about 35%; averaging many analysts after that cuts about 61%.
note: Numbers come from Mandel 2018 only (a-09, b-03, c-04 duplicate it). Karvetski 2020 and Mandel 2015 support the coherence and aggregation gains. b-03: plain normalization (0.13) did as well as coherentization. Human analysts, one task; LLM transfer untested.

claim: Most of the aggregation gain comes from about 3 judges.
note: Appears only in the earlier brief, in no evidence line. Verify before using the number 3.

claim: ACH-trained analysts judged cue usefulness far better (r=.68 vs .17) but final accuracy did not improve.
note: One study seen three times. A trained sub-skill did not carry to the end result.

claim: ACH users show pseudo-diagnostic weighting: non-diagnostic evidence moves them about 30% as much as diagnostic evidence.
note: Karvetski and Mandel 2020 only. Supports a code-side filter that drops evidence fitting all hypotheses.

claim: Humans in ACH trials often did not complete all ACH steps.
note: One abstract seen three times. Basis for the idea that a program could do better than humans; untested.

claim: Hypotheses-in-rows layout reduced confirmation bias; the standard ACH layout did not.
note: Dhami, Belton, De Werd 2024. Abstract read by agent a only; b and c could not open it. Military analysts mostly showed no bias, so the effect may be on students. No layout benefit for credibility sensitivity.

claim: ACH did not reduce adversarial allegiance or change credibility ratings in mock expert witnesses.
note: PLOS ONE 2026 abstract only. Different domain.

claim: The SAT approach lacks validity testing and may cause mirror-image bias; the field has not measured accuracy gains.
note: Mandel and Tetlock 2018, RAND 2016 (snippet), Wilcox and Mandel 2023 (preprint). The Mandel group is also the main source of the ACH nulls, so not fully independent of claim 1.

claim: Heuer's core logic: evidence consistent with all hypotheses has no diagnostic value, and one should seek disconfirmation.
note: One book. Backed outside this field by Platt 1964 and Klayman and Ha 1987 (in the plan, not in these lines). Logic sound; human gain not shown (claim 1).

claim: People and LLMs both prefer confirming tests (Wason 2-4-6); counterexample prompting helps LLMs (rule discovery 42% to 56%).
note: Heuer reports the human effect (citing Wason). Jhaveri 2026 is one preprint on 11 LLMs seen three times. Gain is on a hidden-rule task with test feedback.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction without external feedback is weak; models fail at locating errors, not fixing them.
note: Huang 2023, Tyen 2024, Hong 2023. Supports 'doubt only when a check or a location signal exists'. Mostly preprints and one benchmark.

claim: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or majority vote; gains are often minimal; errors are correlated.
note: Smit 2023, Cemri 2025, Liu 2026, Kaesberg 2025. Mostly preprints.

claim: A minority answer is sometimes correct and majority voting suppresses it (about 1 in 4 divergent cases).
note: One preprint (He 2026). A rate, not a reason to drop voting.

claim: LLMs conform to the majority and are sycophantic, so a critic or judge can be pulled toward the stated answer.
note: Zhu 2024 and Sharma 2023, both preprints.

claim: Devil's advocacy helps in LLM settings (anticipatory reflection +3.5 points on WebArena; group satisfaction up).
note: Conflicts with the self-correction results and our BrainTeaser drop. The WebArena gain is small and has an environment. The 48-person study measures satisfaction, not accuracy. Both preprints.

claim: Devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry improve human group decisions over consensus (Schwenk 1990 meta-analysis).
note: No agent read effect sizes. Existence only. Schweiger 1986 results in the earlier brief came from search summaries.

claim: LLM assistants, and LLM forecasting systems with aggregation and calibration, reach near-human forecasting accuracy.
note: Schoenegger 2024 (n=991, preprint), Alur 2025 (preprint), Mellers 2014 (human tournament: training, teaming, tracking). Calibration and aggregation recur. Mixed human and LLM.

claim: Real analyst forecasts discriminated well but were underconfident; recalibration helped.
note: One dataset (1,514 forecasts), abstract only. Consistent with the conservatism near 50/50 seen in Karvetski 2020.

claim: ACH-inspired or hypothesis-keeping agent designs (AgentCDM, SIA, multi-agent diagnosis) report gains.
note: No usable evidence: abstracts give no numbers (a-25, b-11), or cases are simulated with no human baseline (b-12). Do not cite as support.

claim: Correction to the earlier brief: arXiv 2609.00738 is BASIN (history-biased search), not an ACH or MuSR hypothesis paper; the '89% hypothesis structuring' claim is unfound. No LLM paper was found that tests a full ACH matrix against a plain baseline.
note: One arXiv API search with zero hits is thin evidence of absence.
